newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt expects IMF deal to save $290 million a year.
newsitem.headline: Egypt expects IMF deal to save $290 million a year.

text.p: Egypt expects to save one billion pounds ($290 million) a year in interest from a debt waiver tied to its new agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Finance Minister Mohyeddin el-Gharib said on Saturday.

Egyptian government newspapers said the government would ask its Paris Club creditors to hold a quick meeting on writing off debts worth $4 billion -- a step which has been waiting on a deal with the IMF for more than two years.
The $4 billion is the last tranche of the $10 billion in official debt the Paris Club agreed to write off under an agreement reached with Egypt after the Gulf War in 1991.
It will cut Egypt's external debt to less than $28 billion, compared with more than $40 billion before the government began serious economic reform in the early 1990s.

"It (the IMF deal) reduces the debt burden on future generations, by $4 billion, and at the same time we have been paying about one billion pounds in interest, which will be saved in the near future," the minister told state television.

Gharib described IMF approval of Egypt's economic reform programme as a great achievement which gave the government a chance to concentrate spending on priorities such as education, health and the expensive bread subsidy for the poor.

"We are now on the road to the real take-off for creating new jobs, increasing investment and for successful exporting and in the end raising the standard of living of Egyptians, which is the main aim of the whole operation," he added.
At a meeting in Washington on Friday, the IMF board approved a $391 million loan for Egypt in a show of support for its efforts to speed up economic growth and transform the economy.
Cairo does not in fact intend to draw on the two-year stand-by loan because its foreign currency reserves are ample, at more than $18 billion or about 18 months of imports.
But it did need the IMF clean bill of health to break the deadlock in relations with the Paris Club, which wrote off the previous and second tranche of debt in 1993.
The breakthrough in economic reform came when President Hosni Mubarak appointed a new cabinet under Kamal Ganzouri in January after years of hesitation about privatisation.
In the last five months the state has sold off more of its assets than it had in the previous three years.
It cleared the last big hurdle to IMF approval earlier this month when it cut import duty by up to 25 percent -- the first across-the-board trade liberalisation since February 1994.
These and other reforms this year have made Egypt the darling of emerging market analysts and foreign investment has started to grow, especially into the revived stock exchange.

Other reforms on the drawing board include new laws on investment and labour relations, modernising the banking sector, transforming the general sales tax into a value added tax and simplifying and broadening the income tax system.
But Gharib denied on Saturday that a cut in income tax would be possible in the near future.
Earlier this week the government newspaper al-Ahram quoted him as saying income tax was too high and the government would announce tax cuts "within days".

But in the interview on television on Saturday, he said: "As for income tax, one day, in the long term, when the revenue is plentiful and there is a surplus to provide free services, then why not (cut it)?"
